What Every Fish Keeper Needs to Know About the Impact of Overfeeding

How to Keep Your Aquarium Fish Alive During A Power Outage

facts.fact: Overfeeding is a more common problem than underfeeding.
Too much food is digested incompletely, so fish excrete more waste; this plus uneaten food pollutes the water and means more maintenance.
Fish suffer more from poor water quality than from a lack of food, so it is better to underfeed than to overfeed.
Uneaten food decays and releases ammonia, which is highly toxic to fish and can kill many fish if not dealt with quickly.
Bacteria turn the ammonia into nitrite and then nitrate; high nitrate feeds algae, which can crowd out live plants.
Rotting waste uses up dissolved oxygen and stresses fish; oxygen-poor areas can also produce toxic hydrogen sulfide.
Overfeeding does not make fish strong or healthy; like obesity in people, it weakens the immune system and strains the body.
Excess food adds nutrients to the water that cause algae problems.
Leftover food feeds bacteria and makes the water worse, and too much food can make a betta fat.
Food still on the surface or the bottom 5 minutes after feeding means you have fed too much.
Signs of overfeeding include leftover food after feeding and fish that lose interest in their food.
Overeating can cause constipation, bloating and swim bladder problems.
Owners often overfeed because they are afraid their fish will starve.
Fatty liver (hepatic lipidosis) is common in captive fish; causes include starvation, diets high in carbohydrate or fat, and rancid feed.
After overfeeding, siphon uneaten food out of the substrate, especially around plant bases and decorations.
Skipping food for a day helps digestion after overfeeding.
Cutting back leftover food lowers the risk of ammonia rising in the tank.
Generally feed fish two to three times a day.
A few flakes, granules or pellets per fish is enough, and the fish should finish it all in two minutes or less.
Most aquarium fish should be fed at least once a day.
For maintenance, feed adult fish 3% of their body weight a day; fry and fingerlings can get up to 5% of body weight a day.
Flake food weighs much less than pellets, so the same volume holds a different weight of food.
Carnivores that eat large meals may only need feeding once or twice a week.
Most fish do well on two small meals a day that they eat within a couple of minutes.
Large carnivores such as eels and arowanas usually do best on one or two feeds a week.
Feed nocturnal fish such as catfish and plecos after lights-out or early in the morning.
Juveniles, fry and breeding fish need more food than adults that are not breeding.
Feed only what the fish eat completely in about 2–3 minutes; small meals often are better than large meals rarely.
For pond fish, young fish need at least five feeds a day, while older fish can manage with one feed in the evening.
A large koi weighing 100 grammes needs about 1–2 grammes of food a day.
Find the right amount by increasing it slowly, then use the same measure every time.
Feed a betta once or twice a day, spacing the meals evenly; each meal is about 3 pellets or 3 brine shrimp.
If food is left over, give less next time, for example 3 pellets instead of 4.
Most adult fish benefit from one fasting day a week.
Give a betta one fasting day each week.
Giving frozen meaty foods or vegetables a few times a week can help prevent digestive blockages.
Do partial water changes about weekly to dilute the nitrate that builds up from food and waste.
Reduce how much and how often you feed, test the water before feeding, and change part of the water about once a week or more often.
Store dry food in a pest-proof container somewhere cool and dry; heat and humidity speed up spoilage, mould and rancidity.

Throw away an opened food container kept at room temperature after 2 months; dry food kept in the freezer after 6 months; frozen foods such as bloodworms or brine shrimp after 1 year; never refreeze thawed food.
Feeding more because fish seem hungry: fish learn the routine and act as if it is feeding time whenever someone comes near the tank.
Feeding to excess out of fear the fish will starve is a common mistake; healthy fish need only what they eat in a few minutes.
During a power cut, do not feed the fish and leave the tank alone; fish can usually go a week without food.
After the power comes back, wait about 24 hours or until water quality is normal before feeding, then start with smaller portions than usual.
Heat and humidity make fish food spoil and go rancid faster, so in a hot, humid climate keep it sealed somewhere cool and dry.
UK Pet Food says the belief that underfeeding is the bigger danger is wrong: fish are more vulnerable to poor water than to too little food.
JBL says overfeeding does not produce stronger or healthier fish.
